extracted.intended_audience: general public; historians; prospective grantees and stakeholders interested in Carnegie Corporation history and priorities
extracted.subtask_description: A historical summary of Carnegie Corporation of New York's founding mission, evolving priorities, and patterns of grantmaking from 1911 onward. Useful for understanding the foundation's past funding priorities and governance principles that shaped its giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founding mission: advance and diffuse knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The Corporation was established 'to promote the advancement and diffusion of knowledge and understanding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This foundational mission underlies program choices and signals a preference for activities that increase public knowledge, research capacity, and educational opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority focus: international peace and advancement of education
rubrics_metrics.description: The Corporation has devoted unremitting effort toward the two issues Andrew Carnegie considered of paramount importance: international peace and the advancement of education and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs and grants should align with or contribute to these two enduring priority areas; historically these have been the principal domains for funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustee discretion and adaptability of priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie wrote that 'conditions upon erth [sic] inevitably change; hence, no wise man will bind Trustees forever to certain paths, causes or institutions... I giv [sic] my Trustees full authority to change policy or causes hitherto aided, from time to time, when this, in their opinion, has become necessary or desirable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Corporation expects trustees and staff to exercise judgment and adapt funding priorities over time rather than rigidly adhering to original, permanent commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indiscriminate giving; be selective
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted principle: 'One of the chief obstacles which the philanthropist meets in his efforts to do real and permanent good in this world is the practice of indiscriminate giving.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grantmaking should be strategic and selective rather than broad, unfocused donations; preference for targeted investments that aim for lasting impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for public libraries and public access to learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Early grants followed Carnegie's personal philanthropy pattern: gifts for construction of public libraries continued and libraries were viewed as 'the university of the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, the Corporation funded library construction and initiatives that expand public access to learning; proposals that advance public educational resources align with this legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for educational institutions and agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants historically went to universities, colleges, schools, and general educational agencies as well as other Carnegie organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity-building grants to formal educational institutions and agencies have been a recurring funding vehicle; large institutional grants are within precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for building scientific expertise and 'scientific management'
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Carnegie’s death, the Corporation aligned programs with 'scientific assumptions' and sought to increase scientific expertise and 'scientific management,' building centers of excellence in the natural and social sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals that strengthen scientific research capacity, apply rigorous methods, or create centers of excellence in sciences are congruent with the Corporation’s historical approach to achieving societal improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor institutional capacity-building via large grants
rubrics_metrics.description: The Corporation made large grants to institutions such as the National Academy of Sciences/National Research Council, Carnegie Institution of Washington, National Bureau of Economic Research, Food Research Institute at Stanford University, and the Brookings Institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a historical precedent for substantial, organization-level funding aimed at building long-term institutional capabilities and national research infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest in adult education and lifelong learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The Corporation developed an interest in adult education and lifelong learning as a logical sequel to Carnegie's preoccupation with libraries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs that promote adult learning, continuing education, and lifelong learning opportunities fit within the Corporation’s historical scope of concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic scope includes the United States and parts of the Commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: While Carnegie intended most philanthropy to benefit the United States, he earmarked a portion of the endowment for Canada and what were then the British Colonies (later known as the Commonwealth Program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, funding could be directed primarily to the U.S. but with explicit provision and precedent for supporting work in Canada and Commonwealth countries.
